responses.user_utterance: Eating dinner late at night might be making it worse for me then. Why does acid reflux actually happen, by the way?
responses.user_rubrik: Why does acid reflux happen? Does acid reflux have a reason?
responses.text: Good point — late dinners often do make reflux worse. In short, acid reflux happens when stomach contents move backward into the esophagus because the body’s normal barriers or drainage aren’t working well. Key reasons:  - Weak or relaxed lower esophageal sphincter (LES): the valve between esophagus and stomach should close after a meal. If it relaxes too often or is damaged, acid can escape.   - Increased stomach pressure or volume: large, fatty, or late meals expand the stomach and push contents up.   - Delayed gastric emptying: if food stays in the stomach longer, there’s more opportunity to reflux.   - Body position: when you lie down soon after eating, gravity no longer keeps contents down, so reflux reaches the esophagus and throat more easily.   - Vicious cycle: repeated reflux inflames and stiffens the sphincter and esophagus, making reflux more likely over time.  That’s why smaller meals, finishing eating 2–3 hours before bed, elevating the head of the bed, and weight reduction help. If symptoms persist, see your doctor.

responses.user_utterance: How do those medications actually reduce acid reflux symptoms?
responses.user_rubrik: How do medication for stomach acid reflux work?
responses.text: They work in three different ways:  - Antacids (Tums, Rolaids, Mylanta) chemically neutralize stomach acid on contact. That raises pH quickly and gives fast, short‑lived relief of burning, but doesn’t stop new acid production or heal damaged tissue.  - H2‑receptor blockers (famotidine/Pepcid, cimetidine) block histamine H2 receptors on stomach parietal cells, which reduces the amount of acid the stomach produces. They take longer than antacids (often ~1 hour) but last many hours and are useful for occasional or predictable heartburn.  - Proton‑pump inhibitors (omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole) block the stomach’s final acid‑secreting step (the H+/K+ ATPase “proton pump”), profoundly reducing acid production. They’re the most powerful for healing inflammation and preventing recurrent reflux but take longer (often 1–4 days to reach full effect) and are usually taken daily for a prescribed course.  Choice depends on symptom timing, severity, and whether tissue healing is needed.

responses.user_rubrik: How to make a good coffee?
responses.text: Start with these core elements — they control most of the taste:  - Beans & freshness: use freshly roasted, freshly ground beans. For cold brew, use room-temp or cold water and long steeping. - Brew time and method: steeping/extraction time affects strength and flavor (cold brew 12–24 hours). Adjust time to taste. - Measure and record: use a scale, take notes, and adjust one variable at a time until you like the result.  Start with these, then tweak grind, ratio, time, and temperature to dial in your perfect cup.

responses.user_rubrik: What are the different types of coffee beans?
responses.text: There are four main commercial coffee species to know:  - Arabica (Coffea arabica): The most common. Grown at higher altitudes, slower-maturing—often sweeter, more complex and aromatic. Base for most specialty coffee.  - Robusta (Coffea canephora): Hardier plant, grows at lower altitudes, higher caffeine. Tends toward a heavier body, more bitterness and dark‑chocolate/earthy notes; often used in espresso blends for crema and body.  - Liberica (Coffea liberica): Rare (small % of global production). Large, asymmetrical beans with a bold, earthy/smoky or nutty profile (e.g., Kapeng Barako). Popular regionally in Southeast Asia.  - Excelsa: Historically treated as a separate species but now usually classed as a variety of Liberica. Used mainly for blending to add complexity and tart/fruitier notes.  Note: roast and grind matter as much as bean species—roast profile strongly shapes final flavor and best brewing method.

responses.user_rubrik: When should I add grease on a bike chain?

Routine I recommend: - After every wet/muddy ride: wipe the chain with a rag or baby wipe to remove grit, let it dry briefly, then apply a few drops of wet-specific lube to each roller and wipe off excess from the outer plates. This prevents abrasive dirt from working into the rollers. - Full clean (degrease + deep scrub): every week if you ride daily in mud/wet conditions, or every few rides when it’s frequently wet. If you only get occasional wet rides, a quick wipe+re-lube after each ride and a full clean every few weeks is fine. - Do a full clean sooner if the chain feels stiff, is noisy, skips, or looks heavily coated with grime.
